novelty_reference: supplied compact atlas and its declared under-recall of naval-architecture suppliers; company names are retained only as locator examples where memory is stable enough

memory_leads.memory: Ship design is remembered as a layer partly separable from shipyard ownership: independent naval-architecture/design houses and specialist engineering firms can develop hull forms, general arrangements and vessel concepts that yards adapt or license. Deltamarin- and Knud E. Hansen-type names recur as examples, while major yards and research institutes also maintain internal design organizations.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Design reuse can shorten engineering lead time and shape fuel efficiency, cargo capacity and resale comparability across multiple yards; a design bottleneck can constrain newbuilding response before steel fabrication begins.
memory_leads.precision_note: Specific design ownership, vessel series and corporate lineage require Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Large merchant ships are remembered as relying heavily on low-speed two-stroke engine designs from a small licensor ecosystem historically associated with MAN B&W, Sulzer/Wärtsilä and later WinGD-type lineages, while the physical engines are often manufactured under license by Asian engine builders connected to shipyards rather than by the design owner itself.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: A concentrated design/licensing layer can make engine technology, fuel compatibility and service support system-wide constraints even when shipbuilding capacity is geographically dispersed.
memory_leads.precision_note: Brand ownership and licensing chronology changed over time and must be verified.

memory_leads.memory: Medium-speed engines and auxiliary generating sets form a distinct equipment layer for ferries, cruise ships, offshore vessels and shipboard power systems, with Wärtsilä-, MAN/MaK-, Caterpillar- and Bergen-type names recurring in memory. Their economics differ from the low-speed main-engine licensing model.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Electrical load, redundancy, hotel load and maintenance profile can make auxiliary machinery a major lifecycle-cost driver independent of nominal vessel capacity.
memory_leads.precision_note: Product-family history and ownership changes are not asserted.

memory_leads.memory: LNG shipping is remembered as depending on specialized cargo-containment systems, with membrane systems associated with GTT-type licensing and spherical Moss-type containment representing major historical design families. The containment technology can be licensed into multiple yards rather than vertically integrated into one shipbuilder.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Containment know-how, approved yards and supplier capacity can constrain LNG vessel delivery and conversion economics, linking a technical licensing bottleneck to fleet supply.
memory_leads.precision_note: Exact patents, license terms and market shares require Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Hatch covers, cranes, RoRo ramps, winches and other cargo/deck systems are remembered as supplied by specialist OEMs such as MacGregor-type businesses rather than being generic yard steelwork. Equipment choice can determine cargo flexibility and port productivity.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: A vessel may remain technically afloat but economically impaired if critical cargo-handling equipment is unreliable or unsupported, making supplier serviceability part of effective capacity.
memory_leads.precision_note: Supplier portfolios and predecessor brands vary by period.

memory_leads.memory: Bridge electronics, radar, ECDIS, autopilot, dynamic-positioning and integrated-automation systems are remembered as a specialist ecosystem involving Kongsberg-, Furuno-, JRC-, Sperry- and Transas/Wärtsilä-type lineages. Integration and software support matter alongside the hardware itself.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Mandatory upgrades, obsolescence or software/service discontinuity can force retrofit spending and downtime even when hull and propulsion remain sound.
memory_leads.precision_note: Corporate ownership and exact regulatory adoption dates are deferred.

memory_leads.memory: Propellers, shaftlines, controllable-pitch systems, thrusters and steering gear form a specialist propulsion-control layer remembered around Wärtsilä-, Kongsberg-, Schottel- and Rolls-Royce-marine-type histories. These components interact strongly with hull form and operating profile.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Retrofit or failure in the propulsion train can change fuel consumption, maneuverability and off-hire risk without changing the engine or nominal deadweight of the vessel.
memory_leads.precision_note: Brand lineage is chronologically unstable and retained only as a locator family.

memory_leads.memory: Marine coatings and antifouling systems are remembered as a lifecycle-performance supplier class associated with Jotun-, Hempel- and International/Akzo-type names. Hull roughness and fouling can materially affect fuel consumption between drydockings.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Coating performance links maintenance cycles to effective fuel efficiency and emissions compliance, so drydock timing can have an operating-cost consequence beyond corrosion protection.
memory_leads.precision_note: Performance claims and product generations require Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Ballast-water treatment rules created a remembered retrofit market involving many competing OEM technologies, class/type-approval processes, yard engineering and significant vessel-specific integration work. Availability of a nominally approved system does not guarantee an easy retrofit.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Regulatory retrofit demand can consume drydock, engineering and installation capacity and can accelerate scrapping of older ships when retrofit economics are poor.
memory_leads.precision_note: Approval status and rule deadlines are Evidence-sensitive and not asserted here.

memory_leads.memory: IMO 2020-era sulfur compliance is remembered as creating a specialist scrubber/exhaust-gas-cleaning retrofit chain involving OEMs, engineering firms, yards, steelwork, pumps and class approval, with installation slots becoming a practical constraint for some owners.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Retrofit queues can temporarily withdraw vessels from service, while the chosen compliance technology changes fuel purchasing economics and residual-value expectations.
memory_leads.precision_note: Exact vendor rankings, installation counts and economics require Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Newbuilding contracts are remembered as allocating machinery and equipment through a maker's list or approved-supplier framework, with some owner-furnished or owner-nominated equipment. The yard integrates many third-party systems rather than manufacturing a vessel entirely in-house.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Owner preference, approved vendor constraints and long-lead equipment can alter delivery schedules and capex even when hull construction is on time.
memory_leads.precision_note: Contract terminology and allocation of responsibility vary by yard and contract.

memory_leads.memory: Marine equipment economics are remembered as extending far beyond the original equipment sale: OEM spare parts, authorized service engineers, software keys, overhaul intervals and worldwide service-network reach can influence an owner's choice of machinery. Unsupported legacy equipment can create operational risk even if technically repairable.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: A shortage of critical spares or field engineers can extend off-hire and make some older vessel configurations less liquid in the secondhand market.
memory_leads.precision_note: No claim is made about any specific OEM's proprietary restrictions.

memory_leads.memory: Repair and drydock capacity is remembered as clustering in major maritime service regions including Singapore, China, the Middle East, Turkey and parts of Northern Europe, with large graving/floating docks and specialist labor determining what vessel sizes and repair scopes can be handled. Repair yards are a distinct market from newbuilding yards even where groups overlap.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Drydock-slot scarcity can extend off-hire and bunch regulatory surveys or retrofits, temporarily reducing effective fleet supply without changing the fleet count.
memory_leads.precision_note: Specific yard rankings and regional shares vary by period and require Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Shipping repeatedly uses conversion rather than only newbuild or scrap: tanker-to-FPSO projects, LNG-carrier-to-FSRU conversions, vessel lengthening, cargo-system changes and major life-extension work are remembered as specialist engineering/yard activities with their own contractors and class review.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Conversion can create or remove effective capacity faster than a full newbuilding cycle and can extend asset life when secondhand values or niche demand justify the capex.
memory_leads.precision_note: Individual conversion programs and technical feasibility require case-specific Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Classification societies were already recalled institutionally, but the equipment layer adds a supplier-market function: type approval, plan approval and class acceptance can determine whether an OEM technology is deployable on a particular vessel or retrofit project.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Certification lead times and approved-equipment lists can turn regulation into a real supply constraint rather than a simple compliance date.
memory_leads.precision_note: Approval scope and equivalence differ by class and flag.

memory_leads.memory: The atlas already notes shipbuilding geography and learning curves; a refinement is that yards often reuse standard or semi-standard vessel designs/series. Repetition can reduce engineering cost and construction risk, while first-of-kind designs carry more integration uncertainty.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Series production can accelerate capacity additions after an order boom and can influence secondhand liquidity because sister ships share operating and spare-parts characteristics.
memory_leads.precision_note: No specific yard series is asserted.

memory_leads.memory: The atlas already distinguishes nominal from effective capacity; P004 refines this by treating regulatory and efficiency retrofits as a recurring drydock/engineering queue that can remove vessels from service for non-casualty technical work.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: When many ships face the same retrofit window, fleet availability can tighten temporarily even in an otherwise oversupplied market.
memory_leads.precision_note: Magnitude and timing require exact fleet and yard Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Marine OEMs and automation vendors are remembered as increasingly selling remote monitoring, condition-based maintenance and lifecycle-service agreements rather than one-time hardware alone. Data access and integration can become part of the owner-vendor relationship.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Better condition monitoring may reduce unscheduled off-hire, but dependence on proprietary service ecosystems can also alter switching costs and residual value.
memory_leads.precision_note: Current vendor capabilities are not treated as 2026 authority.

memory_leads.memory: Japan, South Korea and China reappeared constantly while recalling machinery and repair clusters, but the supplied atlas already treats the geographic shift of commercial shipbuilding as a major structural theme.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Retained only as a duplicate boundary signal; P004 adds supplier/integration mechanisms rather than another shipbuilding-country narrative.
memory_leads.precision_note: No new category claimed.

memory_leads.memory: Retrofits repeatedly reinforced the atlas thesis that regulation changes effective fleet supply through downtime, capex and scrapping incentives. That mechanism is already present and is not counted as a new category here.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Retained to distinguish new technical supplier topology from an already-covered regulatory-supply mechanism.
memory_leads.precision_note: No new category claimed.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.assessment: The licensor/licensee structure is clear in memory, but brand acquisitions and which Asian builders held which license in each period are too chronology-sensitive to retain specifically.
The supplier classes are obviously important, but blind recall becomes an arbitrary product catalog before a stable industry-structure insight appears.
Major repair clusters are remembered, but exact yard rankings, dock sizes and historical changes require source-first data rather than memory.
The topic is strategically important, but 2025-2026 technical readiness is current-state information and stale model memory is not authoritative enough to retain vendor-specific claims.

stop_reason: The preset questions were answered with a coherent supplier/integration/service topology. Marginal recall then shifted toward arbitrary component catalogs, exact brand ownership, yard rankings and current alternative-fuel product readiness, which either require Evidence or would violate the sparse-map anti-tunnel rule.

method_observation.observation: Technical-supply probing is high-yield when organized around integration bottlenecks such as licensing, type approval, service networks, drydock capacity and conversion; it degrades quickly when it turns into an exhaustive OEM/component catalog. Future technical probes should stay mechanism-first and stop before vendor enumeration dominates.
